analysis.one_liner: Requires background checks through licensed dealers for all private gun sales.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill; it sat in the Judiciary Committee from February 2023 until the two-year Congress ended with no markup, no floor vote, despite 210 sponsors and cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, licensed gun dealers must run a background check on buyers, but sales between private individuals generally do not. This bill would make it unlawful for a private person to sell or transfer a firearm to another private person unless a licensed dealer first takes the gun, runs the standard background check, and completes the transfer. It would exempt close-family gifts, loans at shooting ranges, hunting loans, transfers of inherited guns, and temporary transfers to prevent imminent harm.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who want assurance that the person buying a gun has passed a criminal and mental-health background check, regardless of whether the sale happens at a gun show, online, or in a parking lot. The stated purpose is to keep guns away from people who are legally prohibited from having them [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Buyers and sellers wanting checked private sales

how_it_helps.text: Closes the private-sale gap: a sale between two unlicensed people would be illegal unless a licensed dealer first takes possession of the firearm and conducts a background check under the existing federal process [S2][S3].
Uses the current NICS background check system rather than creating a new one, and the bill states it may not be construed to create a national firearms registry [S3].

Protects common arrangements: gifts between spouses, partners, parents, siblings, grandparents, aunts and uncles; estate transfers; loans for hunting or target shooting; transfers in the presence of the owner; and temporary transfers to prevent imminent harm are all exempt [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private gun owners and sellers, who would have to bring the gun to a licensed dealer and pay that dealer a transfer fee and wait out the check for most sales outside the immediate family. Licensed dealers gain new business handling these transfers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private gun sellers and casual buyers

drawbacks.text: Every private sale outside the close-family exemptions would involve a licensed dealer, meaning travel, paperwork, a waiting period, and a dealer transfer fee that did not exist for a face-to-face cash sale between two law-abiding neighbors [S3].

The exemptions stop at immediate family: a sale to a cousin, a friend, or a co-worker would require the dealer route, so many law-abiding transactions get more burdensome while the check itself only catches buyers already flagged in government records [S3].

Opponents of universal checks argue the burden falls on people who follow the law, since a person who cannot pass a check can still obtain a gun through theft or an already-illegal street sale; the bill cannot verify claims about that, one way or the other [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real and honest to state: background checks today stop prohibited buyers at licensed dealers, but the same two people can trade a gun privately with no check at all. This bill extends the existing check to that gap, at the price of a dealer visit and fee on private sales. The family, hunting, and emergency exemptions keep ordinary life largely unaffected. The main good-faith objection is that the burden lands on compliant owners while determined criminals are the hardest cases to reach — true, but it does not change that the status quo is the only major purchase in America where no check is required at all.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee never held a markup or vote; the bill sat there from the day it was introduced until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican, introduced the bill on February 1, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].
209 of the 216 House Democrats signed on as cosponsors, plus the Republican sponsor — 210 of 435 House members — yet the record shows no committee action beyond the referral [S4][S5].
The bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died at the end of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private sellers who prefer to trade guns with no check, and opponents of expanded checks generally, keep the status quo intact — no one had to defeat the bill, it simply was never scheduled.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Unscheduled bill kept private-sale status quo

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely one-sided: all 209 cosponsors were Democrats, with the Republican sponsor the lone exception, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would make licensed dealers the mandatory middleman for every private gun sale — a new stream of transfer-fee business, even as the bill's purpose is public safety. The check system already runs through dealers; this locks that in permanently.

A universal-check requirement nudges more sales through the dealer channel, where manufacturers already operate, but it does not directly change manufacturing rules. Any effect on their market is small and cuts both ways.

industries.industry: Private firearms market (informal sales, gun shows, online person-to-person)
industries.note: This is the market the bill regulates away: casual person-to-person sales would require a dealer intermediary and its fees. The industry's interest in continuing unregulated sales runs directly against the bill's public-safety purpose.
